summary.one_line: This is not an equity IPO but a Rs.1 crore Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) donation instrument on NSE's Social Stock Exchange for a Hyderabad cancer-screening charity: buyers get no interest, no principal back and nothing tradable, so it fails as an investment. It may be a reasonable 80G-eligible donation, but the charity's finances and project budget could not be checked against the offer document.
bull_points: A real, long-running programme: a public charitable trust set up in 2013 that runs mobile cancer-screening buses for poor and remote communities (S1, S5, S6), with a reported 61,000+ people screened and 1,000+ early cancers detected in 2025 (S7).

Led by a practising surgical oncologist, Dr Chinnababu Sunkavalli, who is Clinical Director and a senior robotic surgical oncologist at Yashoda Hospitals, Hyderabad, so it has real clinical credibility (S6, S8).

Listing brings SEBI-framework discipline: an Annual Impact Report assessed by a Social Impact Assessor, and quarterly statements on how the money was used (S12, S20). The founder says governance, not money, is the main reason for listing (S3, S21).
The contribution can qualify for a Section 80G income-tax deduction, subject to the NPO's 80G registration and the Act's limits. The trust lists an 80G registration (S5, S13).
bear_points: ZCZP pays no coupon and returns no principal. It cannot be traded in the secondary market, so every rupee put in is gone in financial terms (S10, S13).

We could not read the Draft Fund-Raising Document (S1). The NSE archive timed out on every attempt, so the trust's audited income and expenditure, the project budget and its related-party transactions are unverified.

Public data on the trust disagree with each other: the head-office address differs between sources, FCRA is shown as 'Not Available' on one platform but claimed since 2018 by the trust, and impact is put at '5 lakh screened' versus '1.4 crore reached' (S5, S6, S7).

There is a possible conflict of interest: the founder is a clinical director at Yashoda Hospitals, which the trust names as a hospital partner, and a Yashoda director appears at the trust's flagship fundraising run (S6, S8). The referral and pricing terms are undisclosed in what we could access.
watch_points: Subscription figures over 7-9 Oct 2026, and whether the issue clears SEBI's minimum-subscription threshold (now 50%, earlier 75%), below which the money is refunded (S12).
Whether the final Fund-Raising Document's project budget gives a per-unit cost per screening (S12).
The first Annual Impact Report and quarterly fund-utilisation statements after listing (S12, S20).
Whether the 2026 target of screening one lakh people is met (S7, S8).

reasoning: As an investment the instrument returns nothing by design: no coupon, no principal and no secondary-market trading (S10, S13). Anyone looking for a financial return should not apply. The money only makes sense as a donation, and the only financial benefit is a possible 80G deduction (S13).

The money raised (Rs.1 crore, all fresh, no OFS) goes to scale cancer screening and early detection (S2, S18). That is a worthy aim, but we could not check the line-item budget or per-screening cost in the DFRD (S1). So even as a donation, the case for giving this way rather than giving to the trust directly is unproven.

There is no 'moat' in the investor sense. Mobile cancer-screening vans are an established NGO model; the Indian Cancer Society, for example, ran India's first mobile screening unit (S17). The trust's real edge is a founder-oncologist network and government MoUs (S6, S7), not a defensible position.

Governance is the unresolved issue. The founders appear to be family members, the founder holds a senior role at a partner hospital, and public registration details are inconsistent (S5, S6, S8). Without the DFRD's related-party section, this cannot be cleared.

If you are a donor rather than an investor, wait for the issue to close and the first Annual Impact Report to be published (S12, S20). That disclosure is what the listing is meant to produce, according to the founder (S3).

blocks.text: This is NOT a company share IPO. Grace Cancer Foundation is a public charitable trust. It is issuing Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instruments on NSE's Social Stock Exchange (SSE). These pay no interest, return no principal and cannot be traded in the secondary market (S1, S10, S13). In financial terms, money put in is a donation.

Grace Cancer Foundation (GRACE stands for Global Research and Cancer Education) is a public charitable trust set up in 2013 in Hyderabad, Telangana. It works on cancer awareness, early detection, screening, treatment support, rehabilitation and research (S1, S8). Its SSE registration number is NSESSENPO00165 (S1). Trust registration number 20/2013 and PAN AACTG0090J are listed on the Give.do donation platform (S5).

The trust says it got 12A and 80G income-tax exemptions in 2014 and FCRA registration (which allows foreign donations) in 2018 (S6). Give.do lists 80G and 12A numbers but shows FCRA as 'Not Available' (S5). A donor should resolve this inconsistency before giving.

blocks.caption: Issuer at a glance (from accessible sources)

Not verified; own site lists a 9-person staff team

subsections.title: How it delivers its programmes (the 'operating model')

blocks.text: The core programme is the Cancer Screening Bus. These are mobile units fitted with digital imaging, computed radiography/X-ray and mammography, which run free screening camps in poor and remote areas (S5, S21). The trust says it had deployed 6 mobile screening buses by 2023 (S6).

Treatment is not provided in-house at scale. The trust runs free medical camps with counselling and rehabilitation (S5), says it set up 10-bed ICUs in Nizamabad and Khammam (S6), and names Yashoda Hospitals and Apollo Hospitals Hyderabad as hospital partners (S6). In practice, the trust finds patients through screening and relies on partner hospitals for treatment.

items: Screening: breast, cervical and oral cancer and other non-communicable diseases (NCDs), plus HPV vaccination drives (S6, S8).
Geography: mainly Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, with tribal screening in Araku and Odisha (S6). In February 2026 it expanded to Meghalaya and Tripura under an MoU with the Meghalaya government (S7).
Model name: the 'GCF-WAY Model' of cancer screening for early diagnosis in underserved communities (S7).

blocks.text: As a charity, the trust has no sales. It is funded by donations, CSR money and event fundraising. Its flagship fundraiser is the Global Grace Cancer Run. The 9th edition is on 11 October 2026 at Gachibowli Stadium, with about 35,000 participants expected in Hyderabad, entry fees of Rs.800-1,200, and all proceeds going to screening (S8, S9). Quambiant organises the run and Evernorth Health Services powers it (S8).

We could not verify how concentrated its donor base is, or its split between CSR, individual and foreign funding, because the DFRD's financial pages could not be fetched (S1). One aggregator estimate of revenue was found but appears to mix this trust up with a US charity of a similar name, so we have not used it.
Gap: income mix, top donors and per-screening cost are not verified. These are the numbers that would show whether Rs.1 crore buys meaningful extra screening capacity.

According to ICMR-NCRP projections cited by the government, cancer cases in India were expected to rise from 14.6 lakh in 2022 to 15.7 lakh in 2025 (S14). Oral, breast and cervical cancers, the three the trust focuses on, make up about 34% of all cancers in India (S15).

Screening coverage is still thin. The government reported over 1.2 crore women screened for cervical cancer in 2025, but reports suggest about 72% of women aged 25-50 have never been screened (S15). The trust's mission of finding cancer early among the poor is a real and growing need.

Mobile cancer screening by NGOs is an established model, not a new one. The Indian Cancer Society, which has worked in the field for over six decades, runs mobile detection vans across the country. It launched India's first mobile screening unit and first digital mammography unit, 'The Hope Express', and attracts corporate CSR funding such as LG Electronics' Rs.25 lakh grant (S17). Government programmes also screen people over 30 for oral, breast and cervical cancer (S15).

In the funding market, the trust competes with about 90 NPOs registered on NSE's SSE by May 2026. Fewer than 20 had completed a ZCZP raise, bringing in a combined Rs.44 crore or so by early 2026 (S16). Past issues were small: SGBS Unnati raised Rs.1.8 crore, Transform Rural India Rs.2 crore and Ekalavya Foundation Rs.83.5 lakh (S16).
No investor-style moat. Screening vans, awareness runs and hospital tie-ups can be copied by other NGOs and government programmes (S15, S17).

items: Real advantages: a founder who is a practising oncologist with hospital access (S6, S8); state-government MoUs in the North-East (S7); a strong fundraising brand through the run, with about 35,000 local participants (S9).
Claimed records: several Guinness World Records for screening campaigns and a 2016 Limca record (S6). These show the trust can mobilise large numbers, not that its outcomes are better.
None of this is a regulatory or technical barrier. The 'AI-enabled screening units' are a plan, not a deployed capability (S3).

subsections.title: What could and could not be verified

blocks.text: Material gap: we could not obtain the DFRD (S1), which carries the audited financial statements for the past three years that the SSE requires (S12). We are therefore not reporting income, expenditure, surplus or balance-sheet figures. No reliable secondary source gave them, and we will not estimate them.

SSE eligibility rules set a floor on scale. An NPO must spend at least Rs.50 lakh a year and must have received at least Rs.10 lakh of funding in the prior year (S12). Because the trust is registered (S1), it presumably clears these floors, but that says nothing about its surplus, reserves or cost efficiency.

subsections.title: Operating output as a proxy for scale

blocks.text: Without financials, operating output is the only available measure of scale. The trust reports over 61,000 people screened and more than 1,000 early cancers detected in 2025, and targets over one lakh screenings in 2026 (S7). It earlier reported 50,000+ NCD screenings in 2023-24 (S6). If accurate, 2026 screening would grow about 60% on 2025.

The lifetime figures mix 'screened' (5 lakh) with 'reached' (1.4 crore), and the larger number includes awareness activity (S5, S7). The SSE's Annual Impact Report should give an independently assessed number (S12).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key terms
rows: 100% fresh money to the trust; ZCZP has no OFS
Held in demat form only; cannot be traded in the secondary market

blocks.text: Under SEBI's SSE framework, the minimum ZCZP issue size is Rs.50 lakh and the minimum application is Rs.1,000 (S12, S19). The minimum subscription threshold has been cut from 75% to 50% (S12). If the issue raises less than that, the money must be refunded.

Public statements say the money raised will scale the trust's cancer screening and early-detection programmes (S18). In August 2026 the founder separately set out a broader plan: a Centre of Excellence for Preventive Oncology, fully AI-enabled mobile screening units, national cancer and NCD screening, digital health platforms and research partnerships (S3, S4). That plan is much larger than Rs.1 crore can fund.

blocks.caption: Objects of the issue
rows: Cancer screening and early-detection programmes (stated purpose)
Stated in news coverage (S18); line items not verified (S1 not accessible)
ZCZP proceeds go to the project (S10)

blocks.text: We could not check the DFRD's project budget (number of screenings, cost per screening, vans, geography). SEBI rules link the 50% minimum subscription to projects with identifiable per-unit costs (S12), so the final document should contain one. Read it before applying.

blocks.caption: Founders and key people
rows: Clinical Director and Senior Consultant Robotic Surgical Oncologist, Yashoda Hospitals, Hitec City
Dentist with a master's in Clinical Trials; management representative at ClinSync CRO

blocks.text: The trust also lists an 8-member advisory board, including Dr Nori Dattatreyudu of Weill Cornell, New York, along with patrons and a 9-person staff team (S6). The founder's medical credentials are genuine and relevant. Running a trust that, if its targets hold, aims to screen one lakh people a year is a different, managerial skill, and the team disclosed publicly is thin.

items: Hospital link: the founder is a clinical director at Yashoda Hospitals, which the trust names as a hospital partner (S6). A Yashoda director also appears at the trust's flagship run (S8). Where screened patients go for treatment, and on what pricing, is a related-party question.

Research link: co-founder Dr Prameela Rani Sunkavalli is with ClinSync CRO, a clinical research organisation (S6). Since research is one of the trust's stated pillars, any data-sharing or service arrangement should be disclosed.
Family control: two of the three named founders share the Sunkavalli surname. Give.do lists a trustee as 'Garapati Prameela Rani' (S5, S6). The trust deed and board independence could not be checked.

blocks.text: We could not read the DFRD's related-party transactions section (S1). These links may be routine and at arm's length, but we cannot confirm that. They are flagged here as open questions, not as findings of wrongdoing.

We found no regulatory action or litigation in the sources we could access, but without the DFRD this is not a full check. Basic public records do disagree. The head office is given as Hayathnagar, Ranga Reddy on Give.do and as Ameerpet, Hyderabad on the trust's site. FCRA is shown as 'Not Available' on Give.do but claimed since 2018 by the trust (S5, S6). These may be stale aggregator data, but they are the kind of detail that listing on the SSE is meant to clean up.

After listing, the trust must file quarterly fund-utilisation statements within 45 days of each quarter-end and an Annual Impact Report assessed by a Social Impact Assessor (S12, S20). That is a real improvement in accountability.

subsections.title: Risks for the person putting money in

items: Total loss by design: no coupon, no principal and no secondary market (S10, S13). This is a donation, and the only financial offset is a possible 80G deduction within the Act's limits (S13).
Impact delivery risk: the main risk with ZCZP is that the NPO does not deliver the promised social impact (S10). Screening targets have not been independently verified so far (S7).
Disclosure gap: we could not read the DFRD's audited accounts, project budget or related-party transactions (S1).
Related-party and conflict risk from the founder's role at a partner hospital and family control of the trust (S6, S8).

Scope creep: the stated ambitions (centre of excellence, AI vans, national rollout) are far larger than Rs.1 crore, so this issue's money may be spread thinly or used to support the general budget (S3, S18).
Under-subscription: past SSE issues have been small and slow to attract money (S16). If subscription falls below 50%, the issue fails and money is refunded (S12).
Data inconsistencies across public sources on FCRA status, address and impact figures (S5, S6, S7).

blocks.text: Generic risks such as market volatility do not apply here because the instrument does not trade.

Of these, the first and third would change a decision. The first rules the issue out for anyone seeking a return. The third means even a would-be donor is relying on secondary reporting rather than the offer document.

In August 2026 Dr Sunkavalli presented the listing as an 'institutional transformation' focused on governance, compliance, transparency and measurable impact (S3, S4). He said: 'Every rupee entrusted to us must create measurable social outcomes' (S3).

items: Concrete targets: screen over one lakh people in 2026, up from 61,000+ in 2025 (S7); funds from the 2026 run are to screen one lakh economically disadvantaged people (S8).
Geographic expansion: Meghalaya and Tripura programmes starting February 2026 (S7).
Plans with no timeline or cost given: a Centre of Excellence for Preventive Oncology, AI-enabled mobile units, national NCD screening, digital health platforms and research partnerships (S3, S4).

blocks.text: The screening target is specific and measurable. The infrastructure plans have no capex figures or dates in the sources we could access, so they should be treated as aspirations.

items: Quarterly fund-utilisation statements and the first Annual Impact Report (S12, S20).
Actual 2026 screening numbers against the one-lakh target (S7).
Whether the trust returns to the SSE for later rounds, as SGBS Unnati has done three times (S11).

blocks.text: The issue opens today, 7 October 2026, and closes on 9 October (S18). As of writing, no subscription figures had been published in any source we could access, so there are no day-1 numbers to report. ZCZP issues have no anchor-investor allocation and no grey market premium, since the instruments cannot trade (S13).

Applications are made through brokers using UPI mandates (S13). Since May 2026 companies may meet up to 10% of their CSR obligation through ZCZP subscriptions (S13), so CSR money could drive demand more than retail applicants.
Comparable SSE raises have been Rs.0.8-2 crore (S16), so Rs.1 crore is a typical size. The main hurdle is reaching the 50% minimum subscription (S12).

method: Searched the web on 2026-10-07 and opened pages with WebFetch. KEY FINDING: GCFZCZP is a Zero Coupon Zero Principal donation instrument on NSE's Social Stock Exchange, not an equity IPO. The 'mainboard' label in the brief is kept only for the output format. MATERIAL GAP: the primary document, the Draft Fund-Raising Document dated 16 June 2026 on NSE's archive (S1), was found in search results, but every WebFetch timed out and direct download was not permitted in this environment. So audited financials, the project budget, related-party transactions and the DFRD's risk factors were not read. Issue terms (face value, size, minimum application, dates, advisor) were cross-checked across the DFRD search snippet and at least two secondary sources (S1, S2, S18, S19). The organisation profile comes from the trust's own site and the Give.do aggregator, which disagree on some points; those disagreements are flagged in the report. No income or expenditure figures are reported because none could be verified. Where a page had no visible publication date, the access date (2026-10-07) is recorded. Some sources (S13, S16, S17, S18, S20, S21) were seen only as search-result summaries because the pages blocked fetching. No valuation is included, as instructed, and none applies to a ZCZP. No subscription data had been published at the time of writing.
